sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today's story takes place far from the land of Israel, in the great city of Babylon. Around six hundred years before Jesus, the Babylonian army conquered Jerusalem and carried many of its brightest young people away to serve in the king's palace. Among them was a young man named Daniel.

The book of Daniel shows us how to stay faithful to God in a culture that doesn't share our faith. We'll look at three moments: Daniel's decision about the king's food, his three friends in the fiery furnace, and Daniel in the lions' den. As you listen, think about this: what helps a person stand firm when everyone around them is going a different way?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon chose young men from Israel who were healthy, handsome, and skillful in wisdom, to train them for three years to serve in his court. Among them were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The Babylonians gave them new names: Daniel became Belteshazzar, and his friends became Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. They were to eat food and drink wine from the king's own table.

But Daniel chapter one, verse eight tells us: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank.” Notice the word purposed. Daniel decided ahead of time.

Daniel didn't rebel or make a scene. He respectfully asked the official in charge for a test. “Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.” Pulse means simple vegetables. At the end of ten days, Daniel and his friends looked healthier than all the young men who ate the king's food. God gave these four young men knowledge and skill, and Daniel had understanding in visions and dreams. When the king examined them, he found them ten times better than all the wise men in his kingdom.

Later, King Nebuchadnezzar made a huge image of gold and commanded that when the music played, everyone must bow down and worship it. Anyone who refused would be thrown into a burning fiery furnace. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego would not bow. When the furious king gave them one last chance, they answered: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.”

The king ordered the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The three men were tied up and thrown in. But then the king leapt up in astonishment: “Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.” When they came out, not a hair on their heads was singed, and the smell of fire was not even on their clothes.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
Many years passed. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians, and Darius became king. By now Daniel was an old man, but he served so faithfully and with such an excellent spirit that the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.

The other officials were jealous. They looked for something to accuse Daniel of, but they couldn't find any fault or error in him. So they said, we will never find anything against this Daniel, unless it concerns the law of his God. They went to the king and persuaded him to sign a decree: for thirty days, anyone who prayed to any god or man except the king would be thrown into the den of lions. And according to the law of the Medes and Persians, once signed, it could not be changed.

Now listen to what Daniel did. Daniel chapter six, verse ten: “Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.” As he did aforetime — Daniel didn't start praying because of the crisis. He kept doing what he had always done.

His enemies caught him praying and reported him. The king was very upset, and he worked until sundown trying to rescue Daniel, but the law could not be changed. So Daniel was thrown into the den of lions. The king said to him, “Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee.” A stone was laid over the mouth of the den and sealed.

The king couldn't eat or sleep that night. Very early in the morning, he hurried to the den and cried out, Daniel, has your God been able to deliver you from the lions? And from inside came Daniel's voice. Daniel chapter six, verse twenty-two: “My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me.” Daniel was lifted out without a scratch on him, because he believed in his God. King Darius then wrote to all the people of his kingdom, commanding them to fear and honor the God of Daniel, “for he is the living God.”

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What can we learn from Daniel and his friends?

First, faithfulness starts with small decisions made ahead of time. Daniel purposed in his heart before the pressure came. When we decide ahead of time what we will and won't do, we are ready when temptation shows up.

Second, we can be respectful and faithful at the same time. Daniel and his friends served their kings well. They didn't insult or rebel. They simply would not put anything above God.

Third, strong faith grows from daily habits. Daniel's courage in the lions' den grew out of years of praying three times a day. The prayers you pray on ordinary days prepare you for the hard ones.

And finally, God is with us in the fire. The three friends said, our God is able to deliver us — but if not, we still won't bow. God doesn't always rescue us from trouble the way He rescued them, but He always walks with us through it, just as a fourth man walked with them in the furnace.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
What is one small, daily habit that could strengthen your faith — a set time to pray, to read Scripture, or to give thanks? Think about when and where you could start.

Let's pray. Living God, thank You that You are able to deliver, and that You are with me in every fire. Help me purpose in my heart to be faithful to You. Build in me a daily habit of prayer, so that I'm ready when hard times come. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear about a young queen who risked everything for her people: Esther.
